From egg to jar: a year in the snail beds

The man who keeps our snails walks through one year of them, from the April morning they wake to the November week the last pearls are graded.

TL Taras LysenkoKeeps the snail beds 24 September 2026 14 minutes to read

Contents

The beds
  • Soil, shade and a net
  • Four thousand to a bed
Spring: waking up Summer: the laying
  • Finding a nest
  • Lifting the eggs
Autumn: grading and salting Winter: the quiet months

We keep the snails in eleven open-air beds on the south slope behind the farmhouse, a ten-minute walk from the cold room. Everything in a jar of Perly caviar starts there, and almost everything that goes wrong with a batch can be traced back to a bed: too wet, too crowded, too much sun. So this is a year told from the beds.

The beds

A snail needs three things from its bed: soft ground to dig in, leaves to hide under, and air that never dries out. We spent most of our first season learning how much of each.

Soil, shade and a net

Each bed is a strip of loose, chalky soil 12 metres long and 1.5 metres wide, sown with clover and radish for the snails to eat and shelter in. A fine net on low posts runs round every bed: it keeps the snails in and the thrushes out. Over the north beds we stretch a shade net from June to August, when the sun would bake the top of the soil into a crust no snail can dig through.

Four thousand to a bed

We count about 4,000 grown snails to a bed, or roughly 220 to a square metre. More than that and they stop laying. We learned this the hard way in 2024, when two crowded beds gave us half the eggs of the others.

Spring: waking up

The snails sleep through winter sealed inside their shells, a hand's depth under the soil. They wake when the ground warms past 10 °C, which near Kyiv is usually the second week of April. The first morning is hard to miss: after a night of rain the beds are suddenly full of moving shells, and the clover we sowed in March is gone by lunch.

For the first month they only eat and mate. We feed them twice a day, at dusk and again before dawn, because in daylight they do almost nothing at all.

Summer: the laying

Laying starts in late May and runs to the end of August. A snail digs a hole about 4 cm deep with its foot, lays 80 to 120 eggs in it and covers it again. Each egg is a white pearl 3 to 4 millimetres across. Left alone they hatch in two or three weeks; for caviar we have to find them within a day.

Finding a nest

We walk every bed at first light, slowly, looking for a small round patch of freshly turned soil with a snail resting beside it. A snail that has just laid is tired and does not crawl away, and that is often the surest sign. In a good week of June we find about 300 nests a day across the eleven beds.

Lifting the eggs

Each nest is lifted with a soft plastic spoon into a cold tray, never by hand: the shells are thin, and the warmth of a palm starts them ageing. The trays reach the cold room within twenty minutes. There the eggs are rinsed in cold water, picked clean of soil and counted.

Autumn: grading and salting

By September the laying is over and the work moves indoors. Every egg from the summer is pasteurised at a low heat and then graded by hand on three sieves before it is salted. Batch 14, the one in the shop now, went through the sieves in the last week of October. This is what we look for in a pearl:

  • Size between 3 and 4 mm. Smaller pearls taste of little; larger ones are often two eggs grown together.
  • An even, milky white. A yellow or grey tinge means the nest was found too late.
  • A whole, firm shell. A soft or cracked pearl goes to the kitchen, not into a jar.
  • A clean smell, like a forest floor after rain. Anything sharper and the whole tray is set aside.

The pearls are salted at 3 per cent, enough to keep them and little enough to keep their taste, and spooned into jars of 30, 50 and 100 g. Each jar is sealed, numbered with its batch and labelled by hand. Batch 14 came to 1,240 jars.

Winter: the quiet months

In late November the soil cools below 8 °C and the snails begin to seal themselves in. We stop feeding, take down the shade nets and lay straw over every bed. Until April the farm's work is in the cold room and the shop: the last jars of the year leave in December, and then we wait for the ground to warm again.

People ask whether we miss the snails in winter. A little. But a farm that rests for four months starts the spring with snails that lay well, and that is most of the trade.
